meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).

A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Takes present subjunctive entre after querer que (eu quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
I want you to go in too.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Indicates the interior of a room or space, often paired with lá or para.
Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: Expresses staying in a place or state (ficar sentado, fica no celular).

examples.text: Ela fica no celular o dia todo.
examples.trans: She stays on her phone all day.

meanings.note: Describes posture after estar or ficar (ficar sentado, stay seated).
Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Refers to someone's time or duration (esse tempo inteiro).

examples.text: Seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
I stayed there that whole time.

meanings.note: Placed after the noun (esse tempo inteiro) to emphasize completeness.

examples.trans: I stayed there that whole time.

meanings.note: Past form fechou! / fechou? means deal! / agreed! in everyday Brazilian speech.
Favourite corporate buzzword in estamos alinhados (we are aligned).

examples.trans: The whole team is on the same page.

meanings.note: Affirmative reply; paired with senhor here for mock-obedient office humour.
Polite title; saying sim, senhor to an equal coworker adds mock military obedience.

examples.trans: Are you going in now, sir?

meanings.note: Spontaneous Brazilian reaction when noticing a sudden snag or surprise.
Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Informal masculine noun meaning guy, dude, or man; as a feminine noun it literally means face.
Built from des- + marcar (schedule): specifically cancels a scheduled meeting or date.

examples.trans: I need to cancel our coffee.

meanings.note: A gathering of people for a purpose. Here a workplace meeting; the final diphthong is nasal.

examples.trans: I’m not going to the meeting.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Impersonal completed past houve appears in que que houve? (what happened?).
Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Transitively delays other people (atrasa os outros) or intransitively runs late (a reunião atrasou).
Third-person masculine singular subject pronoun.
A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Irregular verb: present ele vem (he comes), completed past ela veio (she came).

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
Having no obligation or meeting; invariant for gender, plural livres.
Standard verb for having coffee, tea, water, or soup.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
I have coffee in the morning.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Diminutive of café (-zinho) naming Brazil's classic friendly coffee break.

examples.trans: Shall we grab a little coffee?
Would you like a quick coffee now?

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Conditional eu gostaria softens a refusal (I would like to, but...).

examples.trans: I would like to, but I have work.

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Everyday workplace verb for handling tasks, errands, or problems.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.
I need to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Diminutive of coisa (-inha), often used to downplay errands or tasks.

examples.trans: I have to sort out a few little things.
Just one little thing is left.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Built from adoçar / doce (sweet), naming artificial or low-calorie sweetener for coffee.

examples.trans: Do you prefer sugar or sweetener?

meanings.note: Cheerful Brazilian exclamation of delight, used ironically by the exhausted employee.
In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Time adverb; até amanhã is the standard workplace goodbye at the end of the day.
